NATIONAL FOREWORD This Indian Standard (First Revision) which is identical with ISO 2787:1984 `Rotary pneumatic tools -- Performance tests' issued by the International Organization for (ISO) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards on the recommendation of the Sectional Committee and approval of the Basic and Production Engineering Division and percussive Standardization PneumaticTools Council.

The text of the ISO Standards has been approved as suitable for publication as Indian Standard without deviations. Certain terminology and conventions are, however, not identical to those used in Indian Standards. Attention is drawn especially to the following: a) Wherever the words `International as'lndian Standard'. Standard' appear referring to this standard, they should be read

b) Comma (,) has been used as a decimal marker while in Indian Standards, is to use a full point (.) as the decimal marker.

the current practice

This standard was first published in 1988 in two parts (Part 1 and Part 2), and both the parts were covering only data sheets for test reports. This revision, which has been prepared by the adoption of ISO 2787: 1984, will come in existence by amalgamating Part 1 and Part 2 of IS 12563, and will cover test methods, definitions in addition to data sheets for test reports. In this adopted standard, reference appears to certain International Standards for which Indian Standards also exist. The corresponding Indian Standards which are to be substituted in their place are listed in National Annex at the end along with their degree of equivalence for the editions indicated.

3.1.1 total pressure : The pressure measured on the stagnation point when a moving gas stream is brought to rest and its kinetic energy is converted by an iser?tropic compression frOM the flow condition to the stagnation condition, It is the pressure usually measured by a Pitot tube, In a stationary body of gas the static and the total pressures ara numerically equal.

3.2.5 static stall torque : The torque that continues to be developed after a load has stalled the motor. NOTE � The value may depend upon the angular position of the motor

Symbols and units

3.1.8 total temperature : The temperature which would be measured at the stagnation point if a gas stream were brought to rest and its kinetic energy converted by an isentropic compression from the flow condition to the stagnation condition. The temperature rise at stagnation of the gas stream can be neglected if the gas velocity around the measuring point is lower than 30 m/s.

4.1

General

rules

for

letter

symbols

The usa of tha letter symbols given in 4.2 and 4.3 is recommended. The list is formulated in line with the following seven principles : a) the same symbols shall be used for the same quantities regardless of the systam of units; b} for any one quantity a single symbol shall be used with subscripts to indicate readings other than tha primary one; c) the same symbols shall be used for a given' concept regardless of the number of special values which occur; d) letter subscripts shall be used to denote values under special conditions; e) numerical subscripts shall be used to denote values at different points of a cycle; . f) symbols shall be confined if possible to reman letters;

3.2 torque

Definitions

concerning

rotary

air motor

performance

3.2.1 static starting torque : The torque that contintiea to be developed by the motor in response to an application of fluid pressure when the torque load is sufficient to prevent rotation.
NOTE � The value may depend upon the angular position of the motor shaft.. The maximum static starting torque is the value obtained when the angular position of the motor shaft is in the most advant~eous location. The minimum static starting torque is the value obtained when the angular position of the motor shaft is in the least advantageous location.

3.2.2 dynamic starting torque : The peak. torque delivered by the output shaft of the motor in response to an application of fluid pressure when the torque load is sufficient to prevent rotation.

5.3.4 Pneumatic screwdriver~and nutrunners

6.1.3 In general pneumatic tools shall be tested at an effective (gauge) air pressure of 6,3 * 0,15 bar. If the tool has been designed for a different pressure (for example 4 bar) this may be used and shall be stated in the test report. The working pressure shall be maintained under all test conditions.

6.1.4 The point of pressure measurement depends on the type of tool used. (5.1.1) 6.1.4.1 Rotary tools (5. 1.2) (5.1.3) (5.1.4) (5.1.8) (5.1.9) (5.1.10) (5.1.11) (5.2.1} (5.2.2) (5.2.4) (5.2.7) (5.2.8) 6.1.7 Due to same type give mance data for tools (minimum

(see also 6.2.4)

The compressed air working pressure shall be measured immediately upstream of the tool.

6.1.4.2

Percussion tools

With regard to pulsating air flow during performance tests, the length of the connecting hose from the point of pressure measurement to the tool shall be at least 3 m and preferably close to this figure. Hose diameter shall be stated in the test report.

6.1.5 All performance data concerning pressure, number of revolutions and blows, power output and blow energy etc., shall refer to the same running conditions unless stated otherwise.

6.1.6 During the test run of the tool, the quality and quantity of lubricant recommended by the manufacturer shall be used.

manufacturing tolerances, even tools of the different performance data. To obtain perforthe type, it is necessary to test a number of five) and state the arithmetical average value.

6 Methods for measurement of tool performance data
6.1 General rules tools for performance test on

6.2

Pressure

pneumatic

6.2.1 Accurate measurement of the compressed" air pressure to the pneumatic tool is of very great importance since the tool performance is strongly influenced by this factor. 6.2.2 For measurement of air pressure, gauges of any suitable type could be used. The gauges selected shall be of such size and quality that 0,5 % pressure difference of full scale reading can be read easily. The pressures to be read shall fall between one-fourth and three-fourths off ull scale reading. The pressure gauge shall be checked and calibrated as often as necessary to make certain that sufficient accuracy is attained. For the calibration, dead-weight gauges can be used. 6.2.3 The compressed air pressure to the tool shall be measured as total pressure at the inlet of the tool hose as specified in the description of, the tool, 5.1.7. This means that the air shall be at rest without any velocity or have a velocity small enough to give a negligible dynamic pressure. This means, in turn, that the velocity of the air at the point of the supply line where the pressure is to be measured shall not be higher than 15 m/s at 7,3 + 0,15 bar absolute pressure. In order to avoid the effect of pressure drop due to supply line losses, pressure measurements shall ba. carried out with the tool running.

6.1.1 All measurements carried out in compliance with this international Standard shall be performed by competent persons and with accurate instrumentation which is calibrated against existing standards or standard methods. 6.1.2 The performance of pneumatic tools is affected by different ambient conditions such as atmospheric pressure and temperature. Moreover, the temperature of the compressed air influences the behaviour of the tool. Test conditions should be in the range of values given below : � � � Atmospheric pressure Ambient temperature Compressed air temperature 960 f 100 mbar 20 A2�C 20*5�C

During the test run with the tool, the temperature shall be kept as close as possible to the test conditions. Any deviation shall be stated in the test report. Tests shall be avoided if the atmospheric pressure deviates from the given conditions.

5

IS 12563:2001 ISO 2787: 1984

6.2.4 Alowair velocity atthepoint of pressure measurement is achieved by fitting an air receiver between the supply line and theinletof the tool. Thereceiver will also damp the pulsations in the air stream to ensure a correct air flow measurement, A suitable arrangement is shown in figure 1.

If noticeable pulsations are present, they shall be damped before the air stream reaches the measuring device. This can be done by inserting another suitable receiver into the line between the compressors and the measuring device. 6.2.7 Tests carried out in accordance with 6.2.4 to 6.2.6 and with a properly calibrate~ pressure gauge will keep the operating pressure within * 2 O\oof the desired value.

Torque

--.

The measurement of the torque of a pneumatic rotary tool shall be made according to generally accepted test codes or procedures. In such a case, reference to the test code shall be made in the report. 6.3.1 The torque shall be measured dynamometers, torquemeters or brakes. by swinging arm

6.3.2 Swinging arm dynamometers $hall not be used below one-tenth of their rated torque capacity. 6.3.3 A correctly performed torque measurement will give a result which deviates less than * 3 0)6from the true value.

where is the maximum air flow for which the device is in9 Vmax tended, expressed in Iitres per second of free air; p is the absolute pressure in the supply line in bars. 6.4.1 Shaft speeds shall be measured with good, accurate instruments which shall be checked with sufficient frequency to ensure proper calibration. If possible, the total number of revolutions during a certain time period should be measured using a revolution counter free from slip. 6.4.2 If the shaft spaed is measured according to 6.4.1 an accuracy of + 2 YO in shaft speed measurement can be expected.

This corresponds to an air velocity of 15 m/s. When testing percussive tools, the volume of the receiver shall beat least 100 times the swept volume of the tool. The inlet to the receiver and the pressure tapping for the gauge shall be located relative to each other so that the incoming air stream does not impinge directly on the pressure tapping. In many cases the insertion of a baffle plate in front of the inlet as shown in figure 1 is advantageous. A thermometer shall be insarted to check the temperature of the compressed air in the receiver and at the air flow measuring device.

6.5

Impact

energy

The measurement of impact energy from percussive tools is a difficult problem for which many different methods have been proposed. Few of them, however, give a true measure of the actual impact energy. In this International Standard, one method has been adopted and is regarded as being suitable if properly handled and checked. 6.5.1 When the hammer piston in the pneumatic tool hits the working tool, for example drill steel, chisel, etc., a strain wave

6.2.5 Before the set-up is used for testing pneumatic tools, it shall be made certain that the desired effect on the prassure measurements is obtained. This shall be controlled by increasing the air flow slowly to the maximum flow for which the device is intended. At the same time the pressure gauge is observed and its reading shall not change more than 0,5 % during this procedure. This also indicates that the supply line has sufficient capacity.

(strain pulse) is generated in it and travels along it down to the bit end. The strain pulse cart be recorded with suitable apparatus. The strain pulse carried a part of the impact energy of the piston, and the maximum stress level of the pulse is a function of the impact velocity of the piston and hence the energy of the piston at impact. By suitable calibration the relation between the impact energy of the piston and maximum stress level can be determined. For details of this test see annex C. 6.5.2 For percussive tools with rotation driven by the motion of the hammer piston, the rotation mechanism shall be run without any torque applied to the working tool during the testing of impact energy.

6.2.6 It shall also be checked that there are no pressure pulsations in the supply line, for example from the compressors. Such pulsations might introduce errors in the pressure measurement and the measurement of the air consumption.

6

M 12563:2001 ISO 2787:1984

6.5.3 If the impact energy is measured as described in annex C, the measurement accuracy may be estimated at + 10 %.

6.7.2

Percussive

pneumatic

tools

6.6

Blow

rate

In the case of a pneumatic percussive tool the power output of the tool is calculated by multiplying blow rate and impact energy per blow according to the following formula : P = 10-3ef

6.6.1 The measurement of the blow rate can be made with the help of any signal which is clearly related to the number of blows of the tool, for example movements of the working tool or number of stress pulses in the same, pressure fluctuations in the compressed air line in the neighborhood of the inlet of the tool or movements of the working piston or the valve. These different pulses can be recorded by means of suitable pick-ups and recorders with a time marker. By counting the number of signal pulses during a certain time period the blow rate can be calculated.

where P e f k the power, in kilowatts; is the impact enargy, in joules;

k the blow rate, in

hertz,

In the test report the calculated power output of tha percussive tool shall be stated.

6.6.2 Since the blow rate of a percussive tool is dependent upon the reflections of the impact wave at the bit end, the measurement of the blow rate shall be made under normal working conditions for the tool. For example, for a rock drill the blow rata measurements shall be performed during actual drilling in rock.

The accuracy of the calculated power output of the pneumatic percussive tool depends upon the accuracy of impact energy and blow rate according to 6.5.3 and 6.6.3 respectively. The accuracy of the power output can th ua ba estimated to be better than i 12 `XO.

6.6.3 The accuracy of a properly performed blow measurement can be expected to be better than ~ 2 YO.

rate 6.8 Air consumption

6.7

Power

output

6.7.1

Rotary

pneumatic

tools

In the case of a pneumatic rotary tool the power output is calculated from shaft speed and corresponding torque measured in the brake. The power output is : A4xw P=--

6.6.1 The air consumption or volume rate of flow when measured at the inlet to the tool remains constant when the tool is equally loaded regardless of the inlet temperature or small changes in inlet pressure. The air consumption of a tool is generally quoted in cubic metres per minute or Iitres per second of free air and is calculated from the measured inlet flow to the tool converted to a free air at a reference atmosphere of :

-- pressure : 1 bar; -- temperature :20 "C; -- humidity :65 %.

1000

where P &l o is the power, in kilowatts; is the torque, in newton metres; is the angular velocity, in radians per second.

The quoted air consumption can be compared with compressor capacity provided the temperature at the tool inlet is the same as the compressor inlet.

The power is calculated for each pair of values of torques and shaft speed. A diagram of power versus shaft speed is drawn. From this diagram the shaft speed at maximum power can be estimated. At this speed the power is accurately measured. In the test report the measured maximum power and the corresponding shaft speed shall be stated. The accuracy of the calculated power output for the pneumatic tool depends upon the accuracy of shaft speed and torque measurement. With the accuracy mentioned in 6.3.3 and 6.4.2 the accuracy of the calculated power output value ca,n be estimated to be better than + 5 0/0.

6.6.2 The air consumption of the pneumatic tools shall De measured on the inlet side of the tool i.e. in the compressed air line to the tool.

6.8.3 The measurements can be carried out using flow nozzles, other pressure differential devices, turbine flow meters etc., the accuracy and calibration of which is known. The measurements shall be corrected if the conditions in the flow meter deviate from those for which it was calibrated.

6.8.4 With a properly performed measurement of the air consumption, the result of the measurement can be assumed to have maximum deviation * 5 % from the true value.

IS 12563:2001 ISO 2787:1984

Annex Procedure for measurement of impact

C energy by the strain gauge method

C.1

Variant A

The following method was developed for measuring the blow energy of pavement breakers and demolition tools. It can be adapted for other percussive tools such as indicated in 6,5.1.

C.1.1 The essential equipment for the strain gauge method is a rod or normal working steel with strain gauge cemented to it, a suitable electronic amplifier and recording equipment capable of producing the full length of the incident strain wave and also of enabling the coordinates of the wave profile to be extracted.

b) the tool must be firmly held down by a flexible device in order to give the same stability that exists under stable operating conditions when the tool is embedded in the material to be broken up before the latter fractures : the flexible device may take the form of calibrated springs or pneumatic jacks. (The device usad for holding the tool while performing the noise level tests to the ECE Directive also meets this specification. ) The following loading shall be adherad to unless otherwise specified, 1j � Concrete Breakers, "T" or double-handed 500 N down force. � Picks, " D" or single-handed :200 force. :450 to

to 250 N down

C. 1.2

The requirements for the rod are es follows :

a) the strain-gauged rod shall have a shank conforming to ISO 1160 at the struck end and be without area changes. The distance from the measuring gauge to the lower end of the rod shall be long enough to ensure that the primary incident wave is not affected by the reflacted wave at the measuring gauge station; b) the distance from the rod collar to the gauge station shall be long enough to ensure that the reflected wave can be measured without interference by the re-reflected wave from the rod collar.

C. 1.8 Input energy to the tool shall be in line with maker's specification.

C.1.9 A number of incident waves (say 25) shall be recorded and the energy calculated individually (see clause C. 1. 12) therefrom and averaged.

C. 1.3 There shall beat least two strain gauges diametrically opposed on the rod and aligned to measure axial strain. The gauges shall be connected in opposite arms of e resistance bridge so as to eliminate the effect of strain induced bending.

C. 1.4 The rod shall be well guided relative to the machine so that the generation of bending waves is avoided.

C.1 .10 The record obtained under C. 1.9 is in the form of a graph of electrical output against time. It is necessary to convert this to the ordinates of stress against time. This conversion can be carried out from the electrical parameters, such as strain gauge factor," electrical excitation to the strain gauge bridge and electrical output. Since the actual gauge factor may be different from the quoted figure due to gauge fixing inconsistency, a check on the calibration shall be made. One method is by means of a drop test. For the drop test the rod is struck by dropping on to it a short well guided bar of uniform cross-sectional area similar to or larger than the rod. The full incident strain wave is recorded.

C. 1.5 If a tool is adaptable to two shank sizes, test results quoting inlpact energy should also mention the shank size used for the test.

v
R=w -- l+y where V k the velocity of piston at point impact, in metres per second; Q is the density of the rod material, in kilograms per cubic metre; y is the area ratio of the rod to piston;

C.1.6 The absorption device is to be almost reflectionless. The reflected energy should not exceed 20 % of the incident energy, measured as the ratio between the first reflex and the primary incident wave energy to simulate the reflection in an actual application.

C. 1.7

The tool operating conditions shall be as follows :

a) the tool must operate in an upright position on the device (see figure 3);
